Title: Gobind: RM226bil in data centre investments to create more than 4,000 jobs
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia's 27 data centre projects approved under the Data Centre Task Force (DCTF), involving an estimated RM225.97 billion in investments, are expected to create 4,053 jobs.
Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo said 3,523 of the positions would be highly skilled jobs, with most expected to be filled by Malaysians.
"Of these, 89.21 per cent of the highly skilled positions are expected to be filled by Malaysians," he said in a written parliamentary reply.
Gobind said the positions would cover electrical and mechanical engineering, networking, cybersecurity, and data centre operations and maintenance.
He said projects approved under the DCTF were also subject to a minimum local content requirement of 30 per cent. This was intended to encourage Malaysian companies to participate in the growing data centre industry.
Compliance with the requirement is monitored by the Malaysian Investment Development Authority (Mida) through project implementation reports submitted every six months.
Gobind said 84 data centre projects had been approved nationwide as of July, including the 27 approved under the DCTF, which was established in February last year.
Of the 27 projects, 16 are in Johor, 10 in Selangor and one in Negri Sembilan. One has begun operations, while the remaining 26 are under construction.
He said TalentCorp Malaysia is also developing a Data Centre Facility Management Programme to equip Malaysians with the skills needed for data centre operations and maintenance.
Gobind said the government would continue monitoring the projects to ensure the investments generated tangible economic benefits, particularly through quality employment, local business participation, skills development and technology transfer.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: BYD driver brought to court over fatal crash that killed 5-year-old girl [WATCH]
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The BYD Seal driver involved in a six-vehicle crash that killed a 5-year-old girl along Jalan Kuching on Saturday was brought to the court complex to face three charges.
The 24-year-old man, dressed in a green shirt and handcuffed, was escorted to the magistrate's court by traffic police.
He was arrested yesterday after being discharged from a private hospital, where he had received treatment for a concussion sustained in the crash.
He was detained at the Dang Wangi police headquarters lock-up.
He is expected to face charges under Section 41(1) of the Road Transport Act 1987 for causing death by reckless or dangerous driving, Section 42(1) for reckless and dangerous driving, and Section 52(1) for failing to stop and report an accident.
The crash occurred at 3.44pm on Saturday, killing the girl and injuring her father and a motorcyclist.
Five cars and a motorcycle were involved in the collision.
Initial investigations found that traffic was moving slowly from the city centre towards Segambut when the BYD Seal allegedly rear-ended a Perodua Bezza driven by the girl's 30-year-old father.
The impact sent the Bezza, which also collided with a motorcycle, spinning into the right lane, where it struck three other vehicles: a Nissan Almera, a Toyota Alphard and a Perodua Myvi.
The girl, who was seated in the rear of the Bezza, suffered severe head injuries and was pronounced dead at the Kuala Lumpur Hospital.
Her father sustained injuries to his right hand, while the 33-year-old Yamaha 135LC motorcyclist suffered head injuries.
Police later located the BYD Seal driver at the private hospital.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Teenager's death: 14 suspects to be charged today
Article:
GURUN: Fourteen suspects, including two minors, will be charged at the Gurun Court today over the death of a teenager whose body was found along Jalan Harvard here seven days ago.
The suspects, all locals aged between 16 and 24, are expected to be charged under Section 302 of the Penal Code for murder.
The 18-year-old victim was found by members of the public by the roadside with injuries to his head and face.
At a previous press conference, Kedah police chief Datuk Adzli Abu Shah said the teenager had been confined for two days, tortured and had his hair cut with scissors after being accused of stealing a motorcycle.
He said the victim was also beaten with blunt objects until he died. His body was then dumped by the roadside at the location.
A post-mortem conducted on the same day found that the cause of death was head injuries sustained from blunt-force trauma.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: EGH International eyes growth as RM313.5mil order book underpins ACE Market debut
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: EGH International Bhd is banking on a RM313.5 million order book, improving margins and a stronger balance sheet to drive earnings growth as the interior fit-out specialist prepares to make its debut on the ACE Market.
Rakuten Trade Sdn Bhd has assigned the company a fair value of 18 sen per share, based on a forecast price-to-earnings ratio of 12 times, citing its project pipeline and earnings prospects.
The research house forecasts EGH International to register core net earnings of RM12.3 million in the financial year ending March 2027 (FY27) and RM14.6 million in FY28.
The company's outstanding order book comprises 18 projects, equivalent to about 1.7 times its revenue in FY26, providing earnings visibility over the next two financial years, with the bulk expected to be billed in the remainder of FY27 and FY28.
Among its notable projects are the Park Hyatt Hotel at Merdeka 118, valued at RM210.7 million, and the Antara Genting development, worth RM143.2 million.
Its largest outstanding project is Armani Hallson KLCC, valued at RM118.9 million, accounting for about 38 per cent of the current order book. Work on the project is scheduled to commence in January 2027.
EGH International has more than 15 years of experience providing turnkey interior fit-out services, covering design, procurement, construction and installation.
The business contributed about 92.1 per cent of the group's FY26 revenue, with the balance coming from the sale of furniture, fittings and equipment (FF&E) and building materials.
Rakuten Trade said the company's ability to secure more large-scale, high-specification projects would be crucial to sustaining growth, while its planned post-listing debt reduction could improve its capacity to compete for new contracts.
Of the initial public offering (IPO) proceeds, RM14.4 million will be allocated to repay borrowings, strengthening its financial flexibility and tendering capacity.
Following the listing, net gearing is forecast to fall to 0.04 times from 2.42 times currently, giving the company greater balance-sheet headroom to pursue new projects and expand its operations.
Beyond its core fit-out operations, EGH International is investing in infrastructure to support larger projects and broaden its revenue streams.
The company plans to construct a five-storey industrial building spanning 130,000 sq ft in Puchong to house its new headquarters, warehouse and showroom.
The expanded facilities are expected to strengthen its ability to handle larger fit-out contracts while providing a platform for the growth of its business-to-consumer (B2C) retail business.
Operating under the IPO World business and Interior Premium Outlet brand, the company sells FF&E products and building materials directly to consumers.
The segment has gained traction, with B2C sales increasing from RM1.1 million in FY23 to RM5.7 million in FY26.
To build on this growth, EGH International plans to establish a 25,000 sq ft flagship showroom at its new headquarters and open additional showrooms.
It is also developing a partner-based model that would enable interior designers and contractors to access artificial intelligence-powered design software linked to the company's product catalogue.
The initiative could create a new sales channel by connecting interior design work with product sourcing. However, with the model still at an early stage, the retail business is unlikely to be a significant near-term earnings driver.
EGH International's expansion plans come amid an expected increase in demand for interior fit-out services in Malaysia.
Independent market researcher Infobusiness Market Research Sdn Bhd projects the market to grow from RM4.7 billion in 2025 to RM6.1 billion in 2030, representing a compound annual growth rate of 5.2 per cent.
The projected growth is underpinned by property market activity, an expanding hotel supply and rising demand from the private healthcare sector.
These segments offer opportunities for fit-out specialists as developers, hotel operators and healthcare providers require specialised interior construction and installation services.
For EGH International, the key challenge will be converting industry demand into new contracts while maintaining project execution and profitability.
Although its existing order book provides near-term revenue visibility, its ability to replenish that pipeline, improve margins and secure larger contracts will determine whether it can sustain earnings growth beyond FY28.
Its retail and technology initiatives offer additional avenues for expansion, but their contribution will depend on execution as the group scales up its facilities and broadens its customer reach.

Title: United Malacca's RM6.10 offer undervalues assets, says analyst
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: United Malacca Bhd's conditional mandatory general offer (MGO) at RM6.10 per share undervalues its plantation landbank and potential asset monetisation opportunities.
CIMB Securities Sdn Bhd analyst Ivy Ng Lee Fang described the offer as unattractive, noting that it represents a mere 2.2 per cent premium to United Malacca's closing price before the announcement.
"This values the company at just 8.8 times its historical financial year 2026 price-to-earnings ratio and 0.81 times its price-to-net asset value.
"The offer also implies an enterprise value of RM33,449 per hectare," she said in a note.
The MGO was triggered after Prosper Trading Sdn Bhd acquired Great Eastern Life Assurance (Malaysia) Bhd's 13.44 per cent stake in United Malacca for RM171.9 million, raising the offerors' combined shareholding to 47.66 per cent.
Ng said the offerors also intend to settle an outstanding MGO obligation dating back to September 2024 through the current offer and a cash compensation scheme.
She said the offer price did not fully reflect the potential value of United Malacca's estates in Melaka, Negri Sembilan and Segamat, Johor, spanning a combined 2,834 hectares.
The estates have a net book value of RM188.1 million, equivalent to just 62 sen per square foot.
"United Malacca's net cash position of RM312.8 million, or RM1.59 per share, provides further support to its balance sheet," she said.
While the MGO provides a near-term exit opportunity, Ng said the offerors' intention to retain United Malacca's listing would allow investors to benefit from potential future land monetisation.
CIMB Securities maintained its "Buy" call on the stock with an unchanged target price of RM6.93, representing a 13.6 per cent upside from the offer price.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Big Tree launches Santuari Kita for mental well-being
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Big Tree, a Malaysian out-of-home (OOH) advertising solutions provider and a subsidiary of Media Prima Bhd, has launched Santuari Kita, a community-driven campaign to promote mental well-being.
The campaign, under the Ruang Rehat initiative, supports World Mental Health Day and invites Malaysians to share messages of hope, encouragement and kindness. The messages will collectively build a digital garden symbolising compassion, resilience and emotional wellbeing.
Running from Oct 10 to Nov 8, the campaign encourages the public to visit ruangrehat.my and submit original messages of encouragement.
Each message contributes to an interactive digital garden, with every submission prompting a flower to bloom. The garden represents Malaysians coming together to support one another through simple acts of kindness.
Throughout the campaign, selected messages will appear in the digital garden through interactive butterflies carrying words of hope.
At the end of the campaign, the top 12 messages will be showcased on Big Tree's digital out-of-home (DOOH) screens, bringing positivity beyond the digital space and into commuters' daily journeys.
The top three winners will receive prizes worth up to RM5,000, including a water villa stay and spa packages.
Another nine consolation winners will receive cash vouchers in recognition of their contributions to the campaign.
"At Big Tree, we are continuously exploring how OOH can create value beyond advertising.
"Through Santuari Kita, we are transforming our digital network into a platform for community participation, where messages of hope and encouragement become meaningful reminders that inspire Malaysians in their everyday journeys," said Big Tree Outdoor Sdn Bhd chief operating officer Muhamad Fariz Mustafa.
Building on Ruang Rehat, Media Prima's mental well-being initiative, Santuari Kita encourages Malaysians to move beyond awareness and help create a supportive community through positive words and shared experiences.
By combining digital participation with Big Tree's DOOH network, the campaign demonstrates how technology, creativity and public spaces can foster meaningful conversations about mental well-being.
The public can participate by visiting ruangrehat.my.
Every encouraging message helps the digital garden bloom, reflecting Malaysians' collective compassion and reminding them that even a few kind words can make a meaningful difference.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Government agency chairman arrives in court to face land deal charges
Article:
GEORGE TOWN: A government agency chairman with the title Datuk, who was arrested to assist investigations into the sale of eight plots of land below market value, arrived at the Sessions Court here today to face charges.
The chairman, who is in his 50s, entered the court complex about 8.30am.
The nature of the charges was not immediately known, although he was recently detained by the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) to assist investigations into alleged abuse of power.
The allegations involve the approval of the sale of eight plots of land in Seberang Prai Selatan below market value in 2015 to a company linked to an associate, resulting in an estimated loss of RM1.96 million to the state.
At the time, the chairman was arrested alongside four others, namely his brother, sister-in-law and two company directors, during MACC operations in August.
The MACC has obtained approval
to charge the chairman today
under Op Jurus.

Title: Gold steadies after hitting one-week low
Article:
LONDON: Gold prices were nearly steady on Thursday after touching a one-week low in the previous session as hot inflation data boosted expectations of a US Federal Reserve rate hike this month.
FUNDAMENTALS
Spot gold was little changed at US$4,114.57 per ounce, as of 0007 GMT, after hitting its lowest level since Oct 7 on Wednesday. US gold futures for December delivery rose 0.7 per cent to US$4,136.10.
US consumer prices accelerated in September as the cost of gasoline surged, putting an interest rate increase later this month back on the radar.
The probability of a US rate hike this month stood at roughly 32 per cent, compared with 22 per cent before the data, according to CME's FedWatch Tool.
San Francisco Fed president Mary Daly said the US central bank will probably need to increase short-term interest rates further, though she signalled no need for a hike at the Oct 27-28 meeting.
Although gold is viewed as an inflation hedge, higher interest rates reduce its appeal because it does not pay interest.
Focus turns to the producer price index and retail sales data due later in the day.
Among other metals, spot silver was up 0.2 per cent at US$55.72 per ounce, platinum fell 0.5 per cent to US$1,598.96 and palladium rose 0.6 per cent to US$1,100.25.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Klang, Johan Setia record highest API reading at 192
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: A total of 34 areas nationwide recorded unhealthy Air Pollutant Index (API) readings as of 8am today.
Klang and Johan Setia in Selangor recorded the highest readings of 192, according to the Department of Environment's (DoE) Air Pollutant Index Management System.
Larkin in Johor recorded an API reading of 187, followed by Nilai in Negri Sembilan and Bukit Rambai in Melaka, both at 185.
Seremban recorded an API reading of 182, followed by Batu Pahat (181), while Shah Alam and Pasir Gudang each recorded 180.
Bandaraya Melaka recorded 178, followed by Alor Gajah (177) and Putrajaya (176).
Port Dickson and Tangkak recorded readings of 175, while Cheras recorded 173.
Pengerang in Johor recorded 172, followed by Banting (171) and Petaling Jaya (170).
In Perak, Tanjung Malim recorded 166, followed by Seri Manjung at 165.
Kluang and Kota Tinggi in Johor recorded readings of 164 and 163, respectively, while Batu Muda in Kuala Lumpur recorded 162.
Kuala Selangor and Segamat recorded 161 each, followed by Temerloh (156), Samarahan (153), and Jerantut, Indera Mahkota and Kuantan, all at 152.
Kemaman recorded the lowest reading among the areas listed at the unhealthy level, with an API reading of 105, followed by the Serian district police headquarters (125), Seberang Perai (144) and Rompin (146).
Meanwhile, 34 areas recorded moderate API readings.
The API categorises readings of 0 to 50 as good, 51 to 100 as moderate, 101 to 200 as unhealthy, 201 to 300 as very unhealthy, and readings above 300 as hazardous.

Title: Japan's Nikkei tumbles as tech stocks hammered on US rate hike worries
Article:
TOKYO: Japan's Nikkei share average slumped in early trading on Thursday, with technology stocks hit hard after hot US inflation figures sparked fears of higher interest rates.
The tech-heavy Nikkei dropped 3.5 per cent as of 0021 GMT, while the broader Topix fell 1.9 per cent.
Overnight, a hotter-than-expected US consumer price index reading stoked bets that the Federal Reserve will need to raise rates earlier and keep them elevated longer, taking a toll on the highly leveraged tech sector. The US Nasdaq Composite slumped 1.9 per cent on Wednesday.
In Japan, artificial intelligence (AI)-linked stocks led losses, with chip equipment makers Advantest and Tokyo Electron drooping 7.3 per cent and 5.8 per cent, respectively. AI-focused startup investor SoftBank Group tumbled 7.9 per cent.
Of the Nikkei's 225 components, 151 fell versus 73 that rose, with one flat.

Title: OpenAI alleges former employee took files on unreleased device to Apple
Article:
ISTANBUL: OpenAI has accused a former employee who returned to Apple of taking more than 100 highly confidential files related to an unreleased device under development, according to a legal filing submitted Wednesday, Anadolu Ajansi reported, citing The Wall Street Journal.
The filing alleged that the files included engineering and manufacturing data, supplier information and internal project documents, according to The Wall Street Journal.
OpenAI claimed the former employee sent some of the files to himself shortly after midnight on June 2, his final day of a six-month stint at the company before returning to Apple, where he previously worked.
The filing also alleges that the former employee presented OpenAI's product plans to Apple executives, including a vice president of operations in Asia. OpenAI claimed the information may have helped Apple advance its plans for AI-powered products, including smart home devices that it announced Tuesday.
Apple rejected the allegations, saying it found no evidence to support OpenAI's claims. The company also said OpenAI had not responded to its requests for additional information to assist its own investigation.
Apple also accused OpenAI of trying to divert attention from evidence in the dispute that Apple said shows its own confidential information was taken by employees who left for the AI company.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Special budget needed to appoint hostel wardens to curb bullying in boarding schools
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Special allocations should be provided for boarding schools to fund full-time wardens as part of efforts to strengthen student safety and curb bullying, said Majlis Amanah Rakyat (Mara) chairman Datuk Dr Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki.
He said a dedicated budget from the Education Ministry to appoint full-time wardens was important to ensure students could be monitored around the clock, particularly at night when most bullying cases in hostels were reported to occur.
Asyraf, who pioneered the appointment of former military personnel as full-time wardens at Mara Junior Science Colleges (MRSM), said relying on teachers to supervise students after school hours was no longer sufficient, given their existing workload and limited ability to monitor students until the early hours of the morning.
"In reality, how can teachers find the time to supervise these children 24 hours a day? They would have gone home by midnight at the latest, yet most bullying cases in hostels occur after that," he said.
As part of efforts to eradicate bullying at MRSM, a special online session on child-related laws was held for MRSM teachers on Tuesday night.
The online briefing, titled 'Safe MRSM: Students' Rights, Our Responsibility', was organised through a collaboration between Mara and the Human Rights Commission of Malaysia (Suhakam), with 3,800 MRSM teachers nationwide taking part.
The session aimed to clarify the responsibilities of MRSM staff in ensuring a safe learning environment free from bullying and child exploitation.
Asyraf said the need for full-time wardens was not intended to question the Education Ministry's capabilities, but reflected the need for a more comprehensive solution to bullying to ensure residential schools remained a preferred option within the national education system.
He said the existing practice of appointing teachers as wardens, with a monthly allowance of RM300, should be reviewed as the additional responsibility added to their existing workload.
"Teachers not only have to teach during school hours, but their duties extend into the night as they supervise students in hostels.
"That is why teachers' rights and welfare must also be protected. We cannot expect teachers to carry out supervisory duties throughout the night without considering their workload," he said.
Introducing a different approach
Asyraf said Mara had introduced a different approach by appointing former military personnel as full-time wardens, who work daily from 7pm to 7am.
He said the initiative could serve as a reference for the Education Ministry in developing more effective monitoring mechanisms at residential schools under its purview.
Asyraf said Mara was prepared to share its experience and research findings on appointing former military personnel as wardens to assess whether the approach could be adopted at residential schools under the Education Ministry.
A pilot project involving the appointment of former military personnel as hostel wardens was previously reported to have been conducted by Universiti Putra Malaysia's (UPM) Institute for Social Science Studies (IPSAS) at Besut MRSM  and Balik Pulau MRSM.
The 191-page study found positive responses from students, parents and administrators, alongside improvements in student discipline. No bullying cases were recorded throughout the pilot project.
The first phase involved 16 wardens who reported for duty at eight selected MRSM on July 1. Full implementation across all 58 MRSM is scheduled to begin on Jan 1, 2027.
Asyraf said the success of the approach was not a reason for Mara to be complacent, but should instead serve as a basis for evaluating the effectiveness of appointing full-time wardens in curbing bullying at residential schools.
"We are not being biased simply because Mara has appointed veterans or former military personnel as wardens. That is why we asked UPM to conduct a study on the matter.
"The screening process for wardens is also stringent, including checks to ensure candidates have no criminal records. Many former military personnel are still young and energetic," he said.
He said the presence of full-time wardens not only helped safeguard students but also contributed to better discipline and more structured daily routines.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Fed's Daly says rate hikes likely needed, but not urgently
Article:
SAN FRANCISCO:The Federal Reserve will probably need to increase short-term interest rates further to rein in too-high inflation, San Francisco Federal Reserve president Mary Daly said on Wednesday, but she signaled there is no need to do so at the US central bank's Oct 27-28 meeting.
"We are more likely than not to need additional adjustments, but the timing of those adjustments to me is something we're still deliberating," Daly told Reuters in an exclusive interview. "I don't feel urgent that we have to decide with a limited set of information. I think we have the time that we need."
Several of Daly's colleagues have also signaled in recent weeks that the Fed is unlikely to raise rates this month. The Fed's policy rate is in the 3.75 per cent  to four per cent range. Longer-term borrowing costs are even higher, with some — like 7.5 per cent mortgage rates — putting a damper on demand in some parts of the economy.
Daly said she feels financial markets understand the Fed's "reaction function," pointing to how traders responded to data earlier on Wednesday that showed consumer price inflation accelerated to 3.7 per cent in the 12 months through September, a bit faster than economists had anticipated. The Fed targets two per cent inflation by a different, but related, measure.
Though the initial reaction was "robust," she said — rate futures traders quickly piled into bets on an October Fed rate hike — investors "calmed" after parsing the data. Higher gasoline prices drove the overall increase, and underlying inflation, while still sticky, did not take a sharp turn upward.
"Definitely this data point suggests that the risk to inflation remains elevated," Daly said. "The risk to inflation has gone up more, but risks are not realities, and reacting on risk when you have time to make a good decision, to me, feels imprudent."
Daly said the labor market's continued stability gives the Fed room to focus on price stability.
But, she said, "Why force urgency when you don't need to have urgency? Why not take the time to be thoughtful and deliberate? And we have more meetings ahead of us."
Financial market pricing now puts about a 40 per cent chance of a second straight Fed rate hike at the central bank's next meeting, higher than before the data but no longer pointing to an increase as the most likely outcome, as was the case shortly after the inflation report was released.
The markets, she said, "understand that we're committed to price stability, and we will do what it takes to achieve it."
Policymakers "have a responsibility to communicate effectively to the public and be accountable, transparent and clear," she said. "The responsibility is to be crystal clear with people about what your objectives are, what you're accountable for and how you're going to balance the risks."

Title: Woman seriously injured in Penang Bridge crash
Article:
PRAI: A 45-year-old woman was seriously injured when two cars collided on the Penang Bridge heading towards Prai early today, causing one of the vehicles to overturn.
Penang Fire and Rescue Department assistant operations director John Sagun Francis said the department received an emergency call at 3.49am about the accident at Km1.3 of the bridge.
He said the woman was trapped in the driver's seat of a Toyota Hilux when rescuers arrived at 4.02am.
"Firefighters managed to extricate the woman safely before handing her over to the Malaysian Red Crescent for transport to hospital," he said.
He said the woman sustained serious injuries to her head, legs and hands.
"Her husband, 47, who was also in the Hilux, suffered minor injuries to his head, legs and hands.
"The 38-year-old driver of the overturned Honda BR-V sustained minor head injuries," he added.
A total of 19 firefighters from the Prai and Jalan Perak fire and rescue stations took part in the operation, which ended at 5.37am.

Title: The budget beyond the budget
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia's federal deficit is projected to narrow from 3.6 per cent of GDP in 2026 to 3.3 per cent in 2027. Yet the deficit of the consolidated public sector is projected to widen from 6.0 to 7.0 per cent. Both figures deserve attention. They describe different parts of the same fiscal picture.
The distinction matters. An improvement in the Treasury's account does not, by itself, establish that the wider public sector is becoming more resilient. That judgement requires an examination of the institutions through which the state invests, delivers services and carries financial obligations.
One Treasury, a Wider Balance Sheet
The Ministry of Finance's Fiscal Outlook 2027 provides the framework. Its consolidated public-sector account combines general government with nonfinancial public corporations. General government includes the federal government, state governments, local governments and federal statutory bodies.
Transfers among the entities covered by the accounts are eliminated to avoid double counting.
The federal and consolidated deficits must therefore not be added together. The broader account already incorporates federal finances. It reveals the combined position after the necessary adjustments.
A dividend paid between two entities within these accounts illustrates the principle.
It changes where resources are held without creating additional income for the public sector as a whole. Similarly, a grant from one level of government to another is an internal transfer, rather than a fresh source of collective revenue.
The coverage still requires care. The description "government-linked" does not automatically place an institution within these accounts. Financial institutions and investment entities outside their coverage require separate scrutiny of their assets, obligations and potential calls on public support.
Consolidation also needs to be accompanied by attention to individual institutions. A combined surplus can coexist with financial stress in a particular entity. Resources held by one institution may be unavailable to meet another's obligations.
A Surplus Is Not a Free Pass
MOF projects the public sector's current surplus to decline from RM49.6 billion in 2026 to RM29.3 billion in 2027. Against development expenditure of RM191.4 billion, the latter leaves an overall deficit of RM162.1 billion. These published 2027 baseline estimates explicitly exclude new Budget 2027 measures, whose effects must be assessed separately.
A current surplus means that current receipts exceed operating expenditure. It does not establish that sufficient resources remain to finance the investment programme.
The gap still requires financing.
A wider deficit does not, however, prove that investment is excessive. Energy systems, transport networks and essential infrastructure may justify substantial expenditure. The test is whether projects are well chosen, delivered efficiently and financed on sustainable terms. Commercial investments need credible repayment capacity; projects serving public mandates need transparent arrangements for meeting their costs.
For debt sustainability, the primary balance—the overall balance excluding interest expenditure—must also be considered, together with existing debt, borrowing costs and economic growth. An operating surplus alone cannot establish whether debt is on a sustainable path.
The comparison must cover the same institutions: a public-sector balance cannot be assessed against federal debt alone. Nor does a financing requirement necessarily produce an identical increase in debt. The use of cash reserves, transactions in financial assets and changes in asset or liability values can affect the relationship.
Resilience Must Reach Every Institution
External uncertainty makes this broader assessment more consequential. Higher international yields can increase refinancing pressure, depending on domestic financing conditions, repayment schedules and currency exposure. Oil-price shocks may strengthen receipts in one institution while raising subsidy or operating costs elsewhere. Conflict, disrupted trade and severe climate events can weaken revenue while increasing expenditure needs.
The practical questions are straightforward. Which institutions must refinance soon? Which projects rely on continuing public support? Which guarantees could become direct government obligations if conditions deteriorate? Addressing these questions early creates room to respond before financial pressures constrain policy choices.
Malaysia would benefit from giving consolidated accounts greater prominence alongside the federal budget. Clear reporting of investment commitments, financing arrangements and contingent obligations would allow Parliament and the public to distinguish productive borrowing from mounting financial exposure.
Federal consolidation remains a worthwhile objective. Its achievement should be assessed alongside the strength of the institutions that undertake public investment and deliver essential services. Fiscal resilience must extend across those institutions, with each obligation understood and each risk assigned to an accountable decision-maker.
The Treasury's figures begin the assessment. The strength of the wider public sector completes it.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Doing the right things and doing things right
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: In business, success depends not only on how efficiently an organisation operates but also on whether it is pursuing the right objectives. This distinction is captured in a well-known management principle: effectiveness is doing the right things, while efficiency is doing things right. Although the two concepts are closely related, they represent different dimensions of organisational performance. A business may execute its activities with exceptional efficiency yet fail because it is pursuing the wrong objectives. Conversely, an organisation may identify the right opportunities but waste resources through poor execution.
Understanding this distinction is essential for boards of directors, senior management, operational leaders and internal auditors because it influences strategic decisions, resource allocation, risk management and long-term sustainability.
Doing the Right Things: The Importance of Effectiveness
Doing the right things means selecting objectives, priorities and activities that contribute meaningfully to the organisation's purpose and long-term success. It concerns what the organisation should do and whether its decisions will achieve the desired outcomes.
For example, a company may decide to enter a new market because of attractive growth prospects. Before committing substantial resources, its board and management must assess whether the market aligns with the company's strategy, whether sufficient capabilities exist, whether the expected returns justify the risks and whether the investment supports sustainable growth.
If the decision is fundamentally wrong, even excellent execution may not save the investment.
Similarly, a retailer may operate its stores efficiently, maintain tight cost controls and process transactions quickly. However, if consumer preferences shift towards online shopping and management fails to develop a suitable digital strategy, the business may gradually lose market share. Its operational efficiency cannot indefinitely compensate for a failure to recognise changing market conditions.
Doing the right things therefore requires sound judgement, strategic thinking, reliable information and the courage to challenge conventional assumptions.
For boards of directors, such a situation means asking whether management is pursuing the right strategy, investing in the right opportunities and managing the risks that could undermine the organisation's objectives.
Doing Things Right: The Importance of Efficiency
Doing things right means performing activities correctly, consistently and efficiently. It focuses on execution, productivity, quality, cost management and compliance with established procedures.
For example, a manufacturing company may improve production scheduling, reduce material wastage, automate repetitive tasks and introduce quality controls. These improvements enable the company to produce goods at a lower cost while maintaining acceptable quality standards.
Likewise, a finance department may streamline its reporting processes, reduce processing errors and shorten the time required to prepare financial statements.
Doing things right is important because poor execution wastes resources, increases operational risks and undermines customer confidence. Even a sound strategy can fail if employees lack the necessary skills, processes are unreliable or management cannot implement decisions effectively.
Internal controls, standard operating procedures, performance indicators and staff training all contribute to doing things right.
Nevertheless, efficiency must be evaluated in the context of the intended outcome. Producing more goods is not necessarily an achievement if demand is declining, just as reducing expenditure is not beneficial if it compromises product quality, cybersecurity or regulatory compliance.
When Efficiency Becomes a Problem
One of the greatest dangers in business is becoming so focused on efficiency that management loses sight of effectiveness.
Consider a bank that reduces operating costs by closing branches and directing customers towards digital services. The strategy may improve efficiency. However, if the bank fails to consider customer needs, digital accessibility, cybersecurity and service quality, the cost savings may be offset by customer dissatisfaction, fraud losses and reputational damage.
Another example is a company that achieves its annual profit target by postponing equipment maintenance, reducing employee training or cutting essential quality inspections. In the short term, expenses decline and reported profitability may improve. In the longer term, equipment failures, workplace accidents, product defects and operational disruptions may increase.
These examples illustrate a crucial lesson: doing things right does not necessarily mean doing the right things. Efficiency can make a flawed decision more damaging by enabling the organisation to pursue the wrong course of action faster and at a greater scale.
Implications for Boards and Management
Boards should ensure that management does not confuse operational performance with strategic success. Achieving budgets, meeting production targets and reducing costs are important, but these measures alone do not establish whether the organisation is moving in the right direction.
Directors should ask questions such as:
*Are our strategic priorities aligned with changing market conditions?
*Are we investing sufficient resources in future growth and emerging risks?
*Are our performance indicators measuring meaningful outcomes or merely activities?
*Are short-term savings creating long-term risks?
*Should we stop, modify or reconsider activities that no longer create value?
Management, in turn, must translate strategic objectives into practical plans, establish appropriate controls, allocate resources effectively and monitor results.
Internal auditors can contribute by examining both dimensions. They should assess not only whether processes operate efficiently and controls function as intended, but also whether activities support organisational objectives and whether the risks associated with those objectives are appropriately managed.
This does not mean internal audits should make strategic decisions on management's behalf. Rather, it should provide independent assurance and insights that help the board and management evaluate whether resources are being used appropriately and objectives are being pursued effectively.
Achieving the Right Balance
The most successful organisations combine effectiveness with efficiency. They first establish what needs to be achieved and why, then determine how to achieve it with the best use of available resources.
Effectiveness should generally guide strategic direction, while efficiency should improve execution. Both require regular review because business conditions, customer expectations, technology and regulatory requirements change over time.
Organisations should also recognise that doing the right things sometimes requires difficult decisions: abandoning an unprofitable business, investing in preventive controls, improving employee capabilities or accepting short-term costs to protect long-term value.
Such decisions may reduce immediate efficiency but improve overall effectiveness and resilience.
Conclusion
The distinction between doing the right things and doing things right is more than a management slogan. It is a fundamental principle of sound business decision-making.
Doing the right things ensures that an organisation pursues appropriate objectives, while doing things right ensures that those objectives are achieved efficiently and competently.
Ultimately, effectiveness determines whether an organisation is heading in the right direction; efficiency determines how well it travels that path. A business needs both. Without effectiveness, efficiency may simply accelerate failure. Without efficiency, even the right strategy may be undermined by waste and poor execution.
The real test of good management is not merely whether the organisation performs its activities well, but whether those activities create sustainable value for shareholders, customers, employees and other stakeholders.

Title: Electricity tariffs, data centres and haze impact among key issues in Dewan Rakyat today
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The Dewan Rakyat is expected to discuss several key issues today, including increases in domestic electricity tariffs, the economic value of data centre investments, aviation safety and the impact of haze on public health.
According to the Order Paper on Parliament's official portal, during the Minister's Question Time, Azli Yusof (PH-Shah Alam) will seek an explanation from the Minister of Energy Transition and Water Transformation on the factors behind the increase in domestic electricity charges and the Energy Commission's assurance that about 85 per cent of households would be shielded from the impact of the adjustment through the Energy Efficiency Incentive.
Datuk Wan Hassan Mohd Ramli (PN-Dungun) will ask about the Youth and Sports Ministry's assessment of the Formula 1 Gulf Air Bahrain Grand Prix 2026 at the Sepang International Circuit, covering the event's effectiveness, operational preparedness, stakeholder coordination and proposed improvements.
Meanwhile, Datuk Dr Richard Rapu @ Aman Begri (GPS-Betong) will ask the Transport Minister to clarify the safety audit records, monitoring audits and latest inspection carried out by the Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia (CAAM) on the operator of helicopter 80-105 9M-LLF following the crash in Long Lellang.
During the Oral Question-and-Answer session, Rodziah Ismail (PH-Ampang) will ask how the net value added by data centre investments is measured after accounting for resource use, incentives, employment, local content and the country's opportunity costs, following the approval of RM385.7 billion in investments since 2021.
Cha Kee Chin (PH-Rasah) will ask about the Health Ministry's measures to address the impact of haze on public health, including cooperation with the Department of Environment and relevant agencies to monitor air quality, issue health advisories, and protect vulnerable groups.
Chong Chieng Jen (PH-Stampin) will seek an update on the growing misuse of synthetic drugs in Sarawak and the effectiveness of measures taken by the police, while Shaharizukirnain Abd Kadir (PN-Setiu) will ask about proposed amendments to the Environmental Quality Act 1974 to enable companies and importers that repeatedly violate laws on illegal electronic waste to be blacklisted.
Meanwhile, Datuk Willie Mongin (GPS-Puncak Borneo) will ask about efforts to strengthen the legal and policy framework for national unity when dealing with sensitive issues involving religion, race and the royal institution (3R), including a proposal to introduce a comprehensive National Unity Act.
The Dewan Rakyat sitting will then proceed with the first reading of the Adoption (Amendment) Bill 2026, followed by the fourth day of debate on the Supply Bill (Budget) 2027.
The Dewan Rakyat sitting runs for 37 days until Dec 8.

Title: Irene Sofiya murder: Classmate to be charged today [WATCH]
Article:
BATU PAHAT: A Form Four student will be charged in the magistrate's court today with murdering 16-year-old Irene Sofiya Mohd Khairool Faisal at a hall in a secondary school in Yong Peng on Oct 3.
According to the e-Judiciary system, the 16-year-old boy, who was Irene Sofiya's classmate, is scheduled to be charged before magistrate Mustaqim Sukarno at 9am.
He will face a charge under Section 302 of the Penal Code for murder.
It is learnt that the decision to charge him was made after the investigation papers were referred to the Johor State Legal Adviser's Office before being submitted to the prosecution for further action.
Irene Sofiya, affectionately known as Fiya, was found unconscious and covered in blood at a school hall in Yong Peng at about 5.50pm before she was pronounced dead.
The only daughter in her family had reportedly failed to return home after her extra classes ended at 5pm.
A friend who noticed a motorcycle at the school went to Fiya's grandmother's house to ask whether she had returned home.
After learning that Fiya had not returned, her grandmother, aunt and friend went to look for her at the school.
The search ended when her friend found Fiya lying inside the school hall.
Following the incident, police detained the boy, who was also Fiya's classmate, to assist in the investigation.
The suspect has been remanded since Oct 4, with his remand period scheduled to end today.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Israel ex-security chief sues Netanyahu for Oct 7 defamation
Article:
JERUSALEM: The former head of Israel's Shin Bet domestic security agency sued Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for defamation on Wednesday, weeks before elections, in a row over responsibility for Hamas's Oct 7, 2023, attack.
Netanyahu, who polls show is in a tight race to stay in power in the Oct 27 election, has faced heavy criticism from the opposition for failing to prevent the attack, the deadliest day in Israeli history.
Netanyahu, who has cast himself as a guarantor of Israel's security over his decades-long career, has insisted that he could have stopped the attack had the Shin Bet's then director, Ronen Bar, or military leaders called to wake him up on the day of the early-morning assault.
In the 134-page court document, Bar accused Netanyahu of "lying to cover himself" and said it was slanderous to accuse him of "criminal failures" over the attack.
Netanyahu made accusations against Bar "that he knew to be false, with the aim of diverting the debate from his own responsibility for the events of Oct 7", the lawsuit said.
Instead, it was Netanyahu's policies over several years that had "increased the dangers posed by terrorist organisations in Gaza", it said.
Bar resigned in June 2025, saying at the time that "all the systems collapsed" in the security agency and that Shin Bet "failed to sound the alarm".
But Bar said he was resigning to take responsibility as head of the organisation and insists he did warn Netanyahu before Oct 7 of potential threats linked to Hamas.
Bar is seeking three million shekels (around US$968,500) in damages from Netanyahu.
Bar said he telephoned the prime minister's military secretary as soon as signs of a possible attack emerged, but that he did not have Netanyahu's direct number.
"Ronen, are you serious?" Netanyahu responded in a statement issued by his Likud party on Wednesday.
"You had my number on the red line and could have called me immediately, as all security chiefs do."
"How many lives could we have saved if only you had called in time?" he asked.
Hamas stormed into Israel with pickup trucks and paragliders and opened fire at sites including a music festival. The attack killed 1,221 people, according to an AFP tally based on official Israeli figures, while fighters also dragged 251 hostages into Gaza, 44 of whom were already dead.
Israel responded with a massive offensive in Gaza that has killed more than 74,300 people, according to the territory's health ministry, which operates under Hamas and whose figures are generally considered reliable by the United Nations.

Title: Trump's new press secretary faces scrutiny over credentials
Article:
WASHINGTON: The White House was facing mounting questions on Wednesday over new press secretary Katie Zacharia's legal credentials, after a faltering first day in the job when she gave an inconclusive answer about where she had passed the bar exam.
A US watchdog group filed a complaint with the State Bar of California, asking it to investigate whether President Donald Trump's spokeswoman — the public face of the administration — had broken the law by repeatedly presenting herself as a lawyer without a licence.
Campaign for Accountability said Zacharia had described herself as a lawyer during television appearances and listed herself as general counsel of a California-based conservative non-profit organisation.
"Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility," said the group's executive director, Michelle Kuppersmith.
"The State Bar should investigate whether Ms. Zacharia has misled the public about her credentials," she added.
Trump described Zacharia as "an attorney" when announcing her appointment on Friday, but journalists have found no record of her being licensed to practise law in any US state.
"I practised international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials," Zacharia said in a statement to AFP, without clarifying whether she held a US law licence.
Zacharia has not specified where, if anywhere, she was admitted to the bar. Asked by reporters on Tuesday where she had passed the bar exam, Zacharia replied: "When I moved to China."
California's state bar confirmed to US media that it had no record of Zacharia holding a licence under either her married or maiden name.
Zacharia, 41, graduated from Pepperdine University's law school in 2011, but obtaining a law degree does not automatically qualify someone to practise law.
Foreign nationals cannot sit China's bar exam, although they can undertake certain legal work at Chinese law firms.
Zacharia previously worked for a law firm in Beijing, according to her professional profile.
The controversy followed a rocky first appearance as White House press secretary on Tuesday, when Zacharia read extensively from prepared notes during a briefing lasting just 14 minutes.
She took questions from only three news organisations, all considered sympathetic to Trump, and stumbled over some answers, at one point accidentally referring to the president as her husband.
Her performance drew criticism from former White House press secretary Jen Psaki, now a TV news host, who compared it to a "Saturday Night Live" comedy sketch.
Trump, however, praised Zacharia's debut, telling reporters: "I thought she was very good."
Zacharia succeeded Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down in August after becoming one of the most prominent public defenders of Trump's second administration.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Trump says he wants to see Pope 'get well'
Article:
BULLHEAD CITY: US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that he wanted to see Pope Leo XIV "get well" after the pontiff underwent surgery in Rome this week to remove a cancerous tumour.
"I want to see Pope Leo get well," Trump told reporters after addressing a campaign rally in Arizona. "It's big stuff. Anytime you have cancer, but the prognosis seems to be good."
"I just want to wish him well. Get better fast," the president added.
Pope Leo's doctors said on Wednesday that he was out of bed, walking and eating after the removal of a cancerous tumour from his lung.
The 71-year-old now awaits the results of a biopsy to determine whether the cancer has spread.
[[nid:1555775]]
Prayers for the recovery of the Catholic leader, who leads 1.4 billion faithful, have poured in from around the world, from the northern Peruvian city of Chiclayo, where he was bishop for eight years, to his US hometown of Chicago and beyond.
Other global leaders also offered their best wishes, including Britain's King Charles III, who is being treated for an undisclosed cancer and last year became his country's first monarch to pray publicly with the pontiff since the Church of England broke with the Vatican 500 years ago.
Earlier this year, the pope said he had "great love" for the United States, but his calls for tolerance and protection for migrants have often put the Vatican at odds with the Trump administration's crackdown on immigration and use of detention camps.
On Wednesday, Trump also noted that he had spoken to the first American pope's brother, Louis Prevost, in the past.
"His brother's a friend of mine who's a great, he's a fantastic guy, and his wife. You know, they're big Trump supporters," Trump said, adding: "His brother loves him a lot, loves the Pope a lot, and that's good. That's good enough for me."

Title: Defence Ministry opens second career path for veterans
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The Defence Ministry is strengthening its commitment to the welfare and future of armed forces personnel and veterans through the MyBakat Veteran initiative, which aims to benefit more than 15,000 people by 2030.
Minister Datuk Seri Mohamed Khaled Nordin said the initiative underscores the ministry's new approach to ensuring that personnel receive support not only during their service but are also better prepared to pursue a second career after retirement.
He said the ministry is placing greater emphasis on aligning military skills and experience with industry requirements to broaden job opportunities for its personnel and veterans.
"We are moving away from the 'train first, find a job later' approach towards directly matching personnel's competencies with industry needs, relevant training and actual career opportunities," he said at the signing of a Note of Cooperation between the ministry and the Human Resources Ministry to implement MyBakat Veteran yesterday.
Defence secretary-general Datuk Lokman Hakim Ali and human resources secretary-general Datuk Azman Mohd Yusof signed the Note of Cooperation in the presence of Khaled and Human Resources Minister Datuk Seri R. Ramanan.
Also present was Chief of Defence Force General Tan Sri Malek Razak Sulaiman.
A memorandum of understanding (MoU) was also signed by MINDEF, the Armed Forces Ex-Servicemen Affairs Corporation (Perhebat) and the Malaysian Employers Federation (MEF) to facilitate the placement of Perhebat trainees and veterans with companies under MEF for a six-month transition period before they are absorbed into permanent positions.
Khaled said the initiative focuses on career preparation at least two years before retirement, noting that between 5,000 and 7,000 armed forces personnel leave the service each year.
"The strategic collaboration also offers opportunities for military experience and expertise to be recognised as professional qualifications through the Malaysian Skills Certificate (SKM) and Malaysian Skills Diploma (DKM), subject to competency assessments and eligibility criteria.
"It also strengthens the roles of Perhebat and the Malaysian Armed Forces Veterans Affairs Department (JHEV), with support from TalentCorp and relevant agencies, in providing career transition training and access to job opportunities," he said.
He said the collaboration highlights the ministry's efforts to expand the support ecosystem for military personnel through a more structured, integrated approach that responds to labour market needs.

Title: Regulate, tax 'Ali Baba' deals instead of criminalising them, economist says
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The government will table new legislation or amend  laws to curb "Ali Baba" practices and rent-seeking, but an economist believes regulating such practices would make more sense.
Williams Business Consultancy Sdn Bhd founder and director Dr Geoffrey Williams said it would make no economic sense to criminalise Ali Baba practices as making them legal would allow them to be regulated and taxed while adding value to the economy.
He said no money was lost through the practice of  Malaysians subletting licences and concessions to foreigners.
"No money is lost because all economic activity takes place in Malaysia and stays here, mostly in small businesses."
He said money was only lost or sent overseas in "grand corruption" schemes and added that major projects were heavily regulated, limiting Ali Baba activity in big businesses.
Economy Minister Akmal Nasrullah Mohd Nasir had said  existing laws, including local  by-laws prohibiting licence transfers, were inadequate to address the practice.
"The challenge right now is that the practice of selling licences or these 'Ali Baba' arrangements is not defined as a criminal offence.
"Therefore, assessing the need for an anti-rent-seeking law is important to enable the practice to be defined as an offence," he told the Dewan Rakyat.
Williams said criminalising the practice would create more enforcement problems and increase opportunities for corruption.
He said licences and concessions given to Malaysians were assets that should be freely transferable.
"If they want to sell those to Malaysians, they can do it. So why not let them sell to foreigners? If foreigners have money to buy licences and concessions, let them spend it. If they want to run companies, invest and employ people, let them do it."
Williams said  regular renewals would prevent  permanent transfers of licences to foreigners.
Criminologist Kamal Affendi Hashim said parties that awarded projects must be held accountable to curb Ali Baba practices, but maintaining proper oversight  was good to provide checks and balances,
He said while any changes to existing laws were welcome, authorities must prepare for  unintended consequences that may follow strict criminalisation.
"The jail time by itself is a good deterrent. But bear in mind that this same threat will push rent or lease fees higher.
"It may  affect the quality or delivery of the project if the third party decides to proceed and pay."
Kamal said investigators  have various tools and techniques at their disposal to detect suspicious activity and confirm any wrongdoing.
He said a database of  contractors, for instance, served as a primary tool for investigators to verify credentials and  genuine project handlers.
He added that authorities could also obtain financial records after a project was completed to detect  anomalous transactions.
"It is not hard, but it does require in-depth investigation and different techniques."
Kamal added that process control standards dictate that genuine business transactions must remain completely transparent.
"Under these standards, any deviation from established controls must be treated as a red flag unless proven otherwise."

Title: Refugees should not be confined to 3D jobs, says NGO
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR:  The government's proposal to allow registered refugees to work in Malaysia's dirty, dangerous and difficult (3D) sectors is a welcome step, but they should not be restricted to such jobs.
North South Initiative executive director Adrian Pereira said refugees should have the freedom to choose employment based on their skills, qualifications, capabilities and preferences, rather than being confined to low-skilled or  demanding work.
"We welcome it, but it shouldn't be limited to 3D sectors. We cannot assume  all refugees are  low-skilled," he said.
Pereira said the right to work should be guided by International Labour Organisation principles, including workers' right to choose their employment without being forced to take jobs they do not want or are not suited for.
He said any refugee employment programme must be properly organised and planned, with clear government policies and implementation guidelines.
"Workers must also receive at least the minimum wage and adequate insurance protection, in line with applicable labour standards.
"Expanding employment opportunities for refugees should go beyond filling vacancies in sectors facing labour shortages. They should also be treated fairly and allowed to use their skills and qualifications.
"The right to work must include the right to choose," he said.
Malaysian Employers Federation senior adviser for government, media and international engagement Datuk Dr Syed Hussain Syed Husman said allowing  refugees who have passed security screening to work  could help address labour shortages.
However, priority must remain on local workers, followed by efforts to improve productivity and adopt technology before alternative labour sources were considered.
Earlier, Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail told the Dewan Rakyat that the government may allow registered refugees to fill labour shortages in the 3D sectors to reduce Malaysia's dependence on foreign workers.
He said the proposal could be considered based on UNHCR data on about 225,000 people with refugee status.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Tighter scrapyard checks needed to tackle cable theft, says Bukit Aman [WATCH]
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR:   Police will conduct licence or permit inspections at scrap metal yards to cut off the market for stolen copper and cripple cable theft syndicates operating across the country.
Federal police believe  continuous checks at scrapyards are  key   to address the growing problem, particularly thefts involving telecommunications cables.
Bukit Aman Crime Prevention and Community Safety Department director Datuk Seri Noor Hisam Nordin said tackling cable theft required authorities to go beyond catching  thieves  in the act.
"We also need to disrupt the criminal supply chain that allows syndicates to profit from stolen infrastructure.
"Continuous operations and inspections must be carried out by the authorities, particularly police, at all scrap metal yards," he told the
New Straits Times
.
His proposal comes as experts warn that cable theft will remain lucrative as long as criminals have access to buyers willing to purchase stolen copper.
Noor Hisam's recommendation reinforces concerns raised by legal and criminology experts  yesterday that enforcement must target not only the thieves, but also the buyers and middlemen sustaining the illegal trade.
The renewed focus on scrapyards follows a series of increasingly brazen cable thefts, including one in Kampung Melayu Panchor, Seremban, recently.
Four masked men were spotted using vehicles to pull telecommunication cables from underground manholes near a primary school in broad daylight.
Footage of the incident went viral, leading to the arrests of 14 people, including two women, in Labu, Nilai and Dengkil.
Police seized five cars, cable-cutting equipment and three sacks of burnt copper wires.
The discovery of burnt copper highlighted how stolen cables were  processed.
Noor Hisam also proposed a comprehensive security framework to prevent thefts at telecommunication installations and underground utility networks.
He said the issue should be addressed through an integrated infrastructure security and crime prevention framework, which combines surveillance technology, physical access controls, threat detection, intelligence-sharing and enforcement.
"The proposed framework could be divided into two categories, reflecting differences in the locations targeted, the syndicates' modus operandi and the level of security risk.
"The first category would cover thefts at telecommunications substations, towers and other facilities, particularly those in remote, hilly or sparsely populated areas," he said.
He said   telecommunications operators must install artificial intelligence-enabled closed-circuit television systems at high-risk facilities. However, he said not all telecommunications facilities faced the same level of risk.
"Operators should therefore conduct security risk assessments based on location, previous theft incidents, asset values, access routes and the importance of the services provided," he said, suggesting an integrated alarm response protocol involving telecommunications companies, private security firms and police.
He said under the proposed arrangement, information on suspected intrusions or security breaches would be channelled immediately to police district control centres to enable a coordinated response.
Noor Hisam also stressed the need for tighter controls over contractors and maintenance activities.
"The second category would focus on underground cable thefts involving manholes, particularly along roads, in urban areas, industrial zones and utility corridors.
"For these locations installing high-security manhole covers could make unauthorised access more difficult."
He also recommended introducing a digital utility work verification system that would allow enforcement personnel to establish whether individuals claiming to be telecommunications workers were authorised to carry out work.
Noor Hisam also proposed network monitoring and cable interference detection systems to enable telecommunications operators to quickly identify suspicious activity.
He said police should adopt intelligence-led hotspot policing, with surveillance and patrols concentrated in areas identified through crime analysis.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: When home becomes a work problem [WATCH]
Article:
A fall down the stairs, a road crash or even a cat bite can take a worker away from the job - and expose how an accident outside the workplace can still hit the household's finances, writes Intan
Maizura Ahmad Kamal
For most workers, a workplace accident is easy enough to picture: a fall at a construction site, an injury involving machinery, a collision while making a delivery. But some accidents happen nowhere near the workplace and can still follow a worker straight back to it.
A fall down the stairs at home, an injury on a hiking trail or even a cat bite may have nothing to do with the job, yet any of them can leave a worker unable to work, with an empty chair at the workplace and a household suddenly having to cope without its usual income.
That's the gap Malaysia's LINDUNG 24 Jam scheme is designed to address: what happens when an  accident unrelated to a person's job leaves them temporarily unable to work.
In its first three months, Perkeso recorded 6,330 claims under the scheme, with RM9.97 million in  benefits paid out.
Because when a worker cannot work, the distinction between where an accident happened and  where its consequences are felt can become rather academic.
An Ordinary Day Goes Wrong
Some of the cases highlighted by Perkeso show just how far removed an accident can be from the  conventional idea of workplace risk: a young worker in Sabah who fell down a staircase at home, another injured while hiking and a veterinary assistant seriously hurt by a cat bite. Other claims  involved road accidents and incidents during workers' personal time.
Yet the common thread wasn't where the accident happened, but what followed: a worker suddenly unable to do the job that provides an income.
The first three months of claims also point to who may have the least room to absorb such a  disruption: workers earning below RM3,500 accounted for 74 per cent of all claims, according to Perkeso.
Edmund Cheong Peck Huang, Perkeso's deputy chief executive (Strategy and Corporate Social  Security Organisation), said the high proportion highlighted the financial vulnerability of lower- income workers when an accident takes them out of the workforce.
"For a lower-income worker, being unable to work for even two or three months due to an injury  isn't just a temporary inconvenience. It immediately threatens family survival."
In July alone, applications rose to 2,135 from 616 in June, while RM3.45 million in benefits was paid  to 2,508 recipients. More than 90 per cent of claims were processed and approved within five days.
Rent still has to be paid, children still need to get to school, groceries still have to be bought and loan repayments continue to fall due.
The Risk We Don't See
The numbers also reveal a more complicated picture.
As of September, 8.5 million workers, or 87.6 per cent, remained enrolled in LINDUNG 24 Jam, while  about 1.2 million, or 12.4 per cent, had opted out. Of those who left, 52 per cent earned below
RM3,500.
The figures alone don't explain why individual workers chose to opt out, and income cannot be assumed to be the reason. But Perkeso said it has identified an awareness and perception gap around the scheme.
For some workers, Cheong said, the monthly contribution can feel like another deduction from their  pay rather than protection against a risk they may never have to face.
Then there's the familiar thought: it won't happen to me.
For workers who are healthy and active, an off-work accident can seem like a distant possibility  until it isn't. Some also continue to associate Perkeso protection mainly with accidents at the  workplace or while commuting, and may not realise that LINDUNG 24 Jam extends to qualifying accidents outside working hours and unrelated to employment.
Others, he added, believe the claims process is complicated, rigid or slow. The challenge, ultimately, is a familiar one: getting people to think about the risk while it's still only a possibility, rather than after it has become a problem.
What The Claims Revealed
The first three months have also given Perkeso a clearer picture of the risks workers face outside the workplace. Cheong said what stood out was the "sheer volume and everyday nature" of hazards that had previously been less visible within the social security framework.
Claims have involved routine domestic and recreational activities, including falls from ladders during home renovations, serious cat bites, weekend sports injuries and road accidents during personal travel.
The overall volume rose sharply, from an average of about 16 claims a day in June to roughly 69 a day by August - more than four times higher. The experience reinforced Perkeso's view that risks don't stop when workers clock out.
Formal-sector workers spend roughly 33 per cent of their time working, including commuting, meaning about 67 per cent of their time is spent outside working hours.
The point isn't that every minute outside work carries the same level of risk. It's that a worker remains a worker - with bills, dependants and earning responsibilities - even when an accident occurs somewhere that has nothing to do with the job.
When Workers Return
By September, about 10,000 workers who'd previously opted out had returned to LINDUNG 24 Jam.
Cheong said Perkeso had found that greater awareness of risk was a key reason workers returned to the scheme.
He pointed to cases in which workers had opted out and subsequently suffered non-work injuries,
only to find they weren't eligible for LINDUNG 24 Jam benefits because they were no longer participating.
Such cases, he said, had served as "eye-openers" within communities.
The increase in reported claims, together with a simplified online re-entry process, also gave workers a way to reconsider their decision.
It's difficult to know what prompted each individual worker to return. But the broader pattern is revealing: protection that can feel unnecessary when nothing has happened can look rather different after something does.
Safety Net With Limits
LINDUNG 24 Jam isn't intended to cover every illness or situation. It applies to eligible employees for qualifying accidents occurring outside working hours and unrelated to employment, subject to the applicable conditions.
Participation for local employees is voluntary, with the worker bearing the contribution. The contribution rate is implemented in phases, starting at 0.75 per cent, rising to 1 per cent for years three to five and 1.25 per cent from the sixth year onwards.
Cheong said another misconception PERKESO encounters is the idea that social security works like an individual savings account, with contributions accumulating for personal withdrawal. Instead, he explained, PERKESO operates on the principle of social solidarity and risk pooling, with contributions supporting a collective social security system.
In other words, the scheme isn't a promise that nothing will go wrong. It's an attempt to provide protection for what happens when something does.
Accidents And Consequences
A staircase at home may have nothing to do with a person's occupation, just as a hiking trail or a road outside working hours may have nothing to do with the job listed on a payslip.
But if an injury means that person cannot stand behind a counter, operate machinery, drive a vehicle, lift goods, work a shift or simply turn up for work, the boundary between a private accident and a workplace problem becomes considerably less clear.
The workplace is where a person earns a living, but it's only one part of the life that income supports. It pays for food and the roof overhead, household bills, transport, rent and the countless ordinary expenses that continue regardless of where an accident happened.
That's ultimately what the 6,330 claims represent: ordinary working lives interrupted by something that happened outside the workplace.
For a worker who's suddenly unable to earn, an accident at home can become a work problem very quickly; the place where the injury happens may be private, but the consequences rarely are.

Title: Victims' kin get loan moratorium
Article:
Your browser does not support the audio element.
KUALA LUMPUR: The families of 54 Malaysians still missing after the Nepal floods have secured a six-month loan moratorium, easing financial pressure amid uncertainty over their loved ones.
Malaysia Solidarity: Families in Hope (MASFIH) coordinator and spokesman Dr Manivannan Rethinam said HSBC and Public Bank confirmed the relief in writing following discussions with Bank Negara Malaysia on Oct 12.
He said two other banks had indicated they were willing to offer moratoriums and waive penalties, but had yet to confirm whether interest would also be waived.
"Behind every outstanding loan, monthly instalment and financial commitment is a family waiting for a loved one who has not returned home," he said, calling for comprehensive financial relief for the affected families.
MASFIH said the families still faced financial commitments and unresolved legal questions while hoping for their loved ones' safe return.
The group also sought clarification on Nepal's procedure for verifying official details of persons missing in the flood following media reports on Oct 12.
The procedure reportedly sets out how missing persons, including foreigners, are verified through Nepalese authorities and diplomatic missions, following a Sept 30 decision.
MASFIH urged the Foreign Ministry to clarify whether it had received official communication from the Nepalese government on the procedure and what steps would be taken to verify the status of the 54 missing Malaysians.
"After 50 days of uncertainty, the families urgently need clear answers and tangible progress," Mannivanan said.
He added that missing-person verification must be distinguished from legal proceedings concerning presumed death.
MASFIH is seeking an urgent meeting with the Attorney-General's Chambers this week to clarify legal issues, including lawful access to financial records, identifying bank accounts and liabilities, insurance claims and the legal status of missing persons.
"We are not seeking to bypass the law. We seek authoritative guidance so that families can protect their loved ones' interests and manage their affairs lawfully,"  Manivannan said.
The group also renewed its request for a meeting with Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim to coordinate outstanding diplomatic, legal and financial matters across government agencies.
"This request is not about publicity or politics. It is about coordinating unresolved issues so families do not have to navigate these complex and interconnected challenges alone.
"Fifty days. Fifty-four Malaysians still missing. Families still hoping. It is time for clear answers, meaningful relief and coordinated action," Manivannan added.

Title: Mohamad: Malaysians in Saudi Arabia safe
Article:
Your browser does not support the audio element.
PUTRAJAYA: Malaysians in Riyadh are safe and have not been affected by Houthi attacks, said Foreign Minister Datuk Seri Mohamad Hasan.
He said the ministry were receiving daily reports from the Malaysian embassy in Riyadh and consulate in Jeddah on the safety and welfare of Malaysians in Saudi Arabia.
However, Malaysians there have been advised to stay home, avoid public areas and locations that could be potential targets.
They are also encouraged to use the e-Konsular facility to contact the embassy for assistance.
"The embassy is in contact with Malaysians in the country to ensure their welfare and safety," Mohamad said.
It was reported that about 250 Malaysian students in Riyadh, Madinah and Makkah were safe, with lectures continuing as usual.
Following attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, several universities in the city have reportedly moved their classes online.
In Makkah and Madinah, physical classes continue.
Mohamad also said some Malaysians were stranded in Jeddah following the cancellation of return flights, as several airlines, including Malaysian carriers, could not operate.
However, he added that the situation was temporary, with Malaysia Airlines offering affected passengers accommodation at locations designated by the airline and making alternative flight arrangements.
He advised Malaysians without urgent reasons to travel to Saudi Arabia to reschedule their trips amid continued security concerns.
